name: Nghị định 109/2022/NĐ-CP
note: Regulates scientific and technological activities in higher education; Article 20 mandates academic integrity code for all higher education institutions; does not mention generative AI — key legal gap
dinh_nghia: Decree 109/2022/NĐ-CP regulates scientific and technological activities in higher education institutions. Article 20 (Liêm chính học thuật) mandates that all higher education institutions must issue a set of academic integrity rules (bộ quy tắc liêm chính học thuật) aligned with four core values: honesty (trung thực), responsibility (trách nhiệm), fairness (công bằng), and transparency (minh bạch). These rules must address prevention of plagiarism (đạo văn), fraud (gian lận), and fabrication (bịa đặt). This is the primary legal instrument for academic integrity in Vietnamese higher education.
phan_loai: Article 20 addresses three main violation categories: (1) đạo văn (plagiarism) — presenting others' work as one's own; (2) gian lận (fraud) — including data manipulation, exam cheating, and misrepresentation; (3) bịa đặt (fabrication) — inventing data, citations, or results. Critically, the decree contains NO provisions on AI-assisted dishonesty, AI-generated content, or generative AI tools — a major legal gap as of 2024–2025.
lich_su_khai_niem: Decree 109/2022 was issued November 30, 2022 and took effect March 1, 2023. It replaced earlier regulations on scientific activity in HE. The academic integrity provisions in Article 20 were new additions reflecting growing awareness of integrity issues. The decree was drafted before ChatGPT's November 2022 release, which explains why generative AI is not addressed. The legal gap became apparent almost immediately upon the decree's effective date.
ten_truong_hop: Decree 109/2022/NĐ-CP, Article 20 — Liêm chính học thuật (Academic Integrity). Issued by the Government of Vietnam, effective March 1, 2023. Applies to all 500+ higher education institutions in Vietnam.
dien_bien: Article 20 requires all HEIs to: (1) develop and publish an academic integrity code aligned with the four mandated values; (2) establish mechanisms for reporting and handling violations; (3) prevent the three named violation types (plagiarism, fraud, fabrication). Implementation is delegated to individual institutions — there is no national enforcement body or minimum standard toolkit. Most Vietnamese universities adopted internal codes in 2023, but quality varies widely. Turnitin adoption remains low (cost barrier) [uncertain]. ChatGPT became publicly available weeks before the decree's drafting was finalized, creating an immediate temporal gap.
ket_qua_xu_ly: The decree establishes a compliance framework but leaves enforcement mechanisms to institutions. Penalties for violations are defined in separate regulations (Nghị định 04/2021/NĐ-CP on sanctions in education). The academic integrity gap regarding AI has not been formally addressed by amendment as of April 2026 [uncertain]. The Ministry of Education and Training (MOET) issued guidance notes on AI in education in 2024 but these are non-binding administrative guidelines, not legal amendments to Decree 109.
con_so_thong_ke: Applies to 500+ higher education institutions in Vietnam [uncertain exact count]; effective March 1, 2023; Article 20 out of 50+ articles; 4 mandated core values; 3 named violation types; 0 provisions on generative AI. Vietnam had approximately 2.1 million undergraduate students (2023 MOET data) affected by the decree's scope.
hai_cho_nguoi_hoc: The decree's lack of AI provisions creates ambiguity for students about what is permitted. Students report uncertainty about whether AI-assisted drafting constitutes gian lận (fraud) under Article 20. This ambiguity — compounded by inconsistent institutional policies — undermines genuine skill development and creates arbitrary enforcement outcomes depending on which institution or instructor a student has.
hai_cho_nghien_cuu: The fabrication (bịa đặt) provision in Article 20 theoretically covers hallucinated AI citations, but without explicit AI coverage, enforcement is legally uncertain. Vietnamese researchers using ChatGPT for literature synthesis may generate fabricated references — a documented risk — without clear legal liability under current decree text.
hai_cho_xa_hoi: The decree establishes Vietnam's normative commitment to academic integrity but the AI gap means Vietnamese degrees may be perceived as less rigorously validated if AI fraud is not regulated. International research partnerships may be complicated by questions about Vietnamese research integrity standards relative to EU AI Act or US NSF integrity requirements.
cong_cu_phat_hien: Decree 109 does not mandate specific detection tools. Institutional adoption of Turnitin, iThenticate, and AI detection tools is voluntary and uncoordinated. Cost barriers limit detection tool access for most Vietnamese HEIs. GPTZero, Turnitin AI Detection, and Copyleaks are used by some institutions informally but with no national policy framework.
han_che_cong_cu: Without legal requirements for detection tool adoption or accuracy standards, Vietnamese institutions face implementation disparities. Detection tools' ESL bias (Liang et al. Stanford 2023 found 61.3% false positive rate on TOEFL essays) is particularly relevant for Vietnamese students writing in English — any AI detection enforcement in English-medium programs risks systematic unfairness.
watermarking: Not mentioned in the decree; no Vietnamese legal or policy framework addresses LLM watermarking as of 2025 [uncertain]. If OpenAI or Google implement watermarking, Vietnamese institutions would need separate policy guidance to leverage it — not covered by current Decree 109 provisions.
thiet_ke_bai_tap: The decree establishes minimum standards (integrity code, violation categories) but does not address assessment design. Process-based assessment, oral defense, and staged submissions are recommended by academic integrity researchers as AI-resistant alternatives but are not required or incentivized under Decree 109.
chinh_sach_truong_hoc: Each HEI must develop its own code. Post-decree, major Vietnamese universities adopted varying approaches: some explicitly prohibited AI tools; others adopted disclosure frameworks. HCMUFA (Đại học Mỹ thuật TP.HCM) issued an explicit AI ban, enforced by 50% score deduction (first publicly reported case, 2023). VNU (Vietnam National University) published AI disclosure guidelines in 2024 [uncertain details].
van_hoa_to_chuc: The decree takes a compliance-mandate approach rather than values-culture approach. Without national support for honor code culture-building (McCabe model) or professional development for faculty on AI integrity, institutional codes risk being formalistic rather than effective.
ai_literacy: Decree 109 does not address AI literacy. There is no provision requiring students or faculty to receive education on responsible AI use. This is a second-order gap: not only is AI fraud undefined, but the regulatory framework does not create a pathway for AI literacy education as part of academic integrity programs.
khung_quoc_te: Decree 109/2022 aligns structurally with international norms (four values overlap with ICAI 6 values) but lacks the specificity of UNESCO 2023 GenAI guidance or EU AI Act Article 50 (disclosure obligations for AI-generated content). Vietnam is not a signatory to the EU AI Act and has no equivalent multilateral AI integrity commitment.
phap_luat_viet_nam: This IS the primary Vietnamese legal instrument for academic integrity. Key gap: Article 20 covers plagiarism, fraud, and fabrication but does NOT address AI-generated content, generative AI tools, or AI-assisted writing. A 2025 amendment or new Ministerial Circular would be required to close this gap. Luật KH&CN 2025 (pending as of 2024) may address some aspects [uncertain].
chinh_sach_chau_a: Vietnam's Decree 109 is less specific than Singapore's NUS/NTU disclosure frameworks (which explicitly address AI) and less punitive than CUHK's expulsion-level sanctions. Vietnam's approach reflects a middle path: institutional discretion within a national compliance framework. The AI gap is the most significant divergence from leading Asian HE systems.
ai_tutor_vs_ai_cheater: The decree's current text implies AI use is governed by the existing fraud and plagiarism categories — suggesting a 'cheater' framing by default. A regulatory update framing AI as a tool with disclosure requirements would shift toward the 'tutor' model that enables responsible integration.
edtech_company_policies: Vietnamese EdTech companies (FPT Education, Topica) and international platforms (Coursera, Google) operating in Vietnam operate outside the scope of Decree 109 — the decree applies to HEIs, not EdTech providers. This creates a policy gap where platform-level AI integration (e.g., FPT's AI tutoring tools) is unregulated from an academic integrity perspective.
de_xuat_nha_nghien_cuu: As an EdTech researcher: (1) Advocate for an urgent MOET Circular amending Decree 109/2022 to explicitly define AI-assisted content and establish disclosure standards; (2) Propose that Vietnam adopt NUS-style AIAS (AI Attribution Standard) as a model; (3) Require AI literacy training as part of the integrity code mandate; (4) Establish national minimum standards for detection tool use, including bias audit requirements for ESL/Vietnamese-language contexts; (5) Create a national case reporting system to document AI integrity violations (analogous to ORI in the US).
bai_bao_khoa_hoc: Nguyen et al. (2024) Springer — AI cheating prevalence among Vietnamese undergraduates, doi:10.1007/s10639-024-12495-4. No peer-reviewed analysis of Decree 109 Article 20 in relation to AI found in Vietnamese academic databases as of 2024 [uncertain].
sach_tham_khao: Nghị định 109/2022/NĐ-CP (full text). Nghị định 04/2021/NĐ-CP (sanctions framework). Eaton, S.E. (2024) Second Handbook of Academic Integrity — provides comparative framework for analyzing Decree 109's strengths and gaps.
nguon_viet_nam: Primary source: vanban.chinhphu.vn/?docid=207110. Secondary: VietnamNet reporting on AI integrity enforcement (2023). HCMUFA case (2023) — first enforcement action under Decree 109-era policies. MOET administrative guidance on AI in education (2024, non-binding).
